newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Mothercare hit by sportswear craze.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Mothercare hit by sportswear craze.

text.p: Retailer Storehouse Plc said on Thursday its Mothercare chain, the UK market leader in childrenswear, had probably lost some market share because of the current craze for branded sportswear for children.
Chief executive Keith Edelman said this had led to a shift in the childrenswear market from traditional retailers to sportswear shops.
He estimated that the overall childrenswear, market, excluding the sportswear sector, had fallen by about three percent on a like-for-like basis over the past year.
Edelman told Reuters in an interview Storehouse planned to introduce sports fashion into its own- brand products to try and capture some of the demand for sports fashion.
"We've got some...ideas in some of our Childrens World stores about how we can capture some of that marketplace," he said by telephone.
Edelman said Mothercare had lost share in the two to five age group, but had held share in the nought to two year old range. Bhs had also held its share in childrens clothing, he said.
Mothercare's sales fell 3.3 percent on a like-for-like basis in the year to March 30 1997, but gross margins improved and profits were up 10.7 percent to 26.8 million stg.
In the eight weeks since the end of March, Mothercare's total UK sales, excluding Childrens World, were up 5.7 percent. Edelman said its sales were also up on a like-for-like basis.
Edelman said the intergration of Childrens World stores, bought from Boots Co Plc last year, was going well.

He said six had been converted to the Mothercare format and another 30 would follow in the current year. (There are 57 Childrens World stores in total). A completely new concept for the largest stores would be tested in the autumn.
Storehouse, which earlier reported a nine percent increase in annual profits to 118.3 million stg, expects to spend 120 million stg on expansion and upgrading stores.

Finance director Chris Martin said about 30 million stg would be spent on adding four new Bhs stores this year and about 15 million on converting Childrens World. Redesigning Bhs to the new "Millenium" format would cost between 25 and 30 million stg and investment in new systems another 25 to 30 million.
The group also expects to take on about 1,000 new staff. Asked about the new Labour government's plans for a minimum wage, Edelman said this was not a worry.
But he said since the minimum wage was unlikely to take account of additional benefits -- such as pensions -- this might mean some adjustments.

"Clearly if they set the wage very high then we'll have to adjust compensation for our staff... to take away some ofthe benefits and put into the wage," he said. He declined to comment on precise numbers.
Edelman said the Bhs Millenium format was doing well, and was driving sales gains. The company plans to finish refurbishing almost the entire 283 store chain by the end of the current financial year.

Bhs's gross margins were down last year due to the downturn in the childrenswear market, he said. "We had more stock to clear at the end of the year than we normally have," Edelman said, "that was the main reason why our margins were down a bit."
Bhs increased operating profit by 14.1 percent to 88.3 million stg. Like-for-like sales were up 3.1 percent.
In the past eight weeks Bhs's sales rose by 6.7 percent and were also ahead on a like for like basis, Edelman said.
Storehouse's shares were boosted by its overall performance in the past eight weeks and were 12.5 pence higher at 229 pence by 0900 GMT. -- Jane Merriman, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
